On September 11, 2026, I presented "The Inertia Apparatus: Furnishing Repose and Refusal" as part of the “Intellectual Furniture: A (Pre-)History of Large Language Models” conference at the University of Basel.

 

This talk is an experiment in conceptual joinery: it dovetails a decade-long research project about the intellectual history of furniture design with a more immediate and embodied concern about the politics of automation and exhaustion in academic labor. Both fields — furniture manufacturing and higher education — have prioritized the creation of apparatae to maximize efficiency and productivity. But when we reach the limits of our cognitive and physical capacity, when we exhaust our storage space, we often assume that personal remedies (e.g., boundary-setting, task-management tools) will solve systemic crises. In this talk I’ll survey recent research on burnout, workload inequity, and the attrition of senior women in the academy — all of which contextualize my own recent decision to resign prematurely from a full professorship. Simultaneously, I’ll explore the politics of labor, pleasures, and existential values and eschatologies embodied in furnishings that empower the idler and outfit the quitter. Think: beds, chaises longues, pool floats, and artists’ furnishings built for dysfunction. How might we design strategies and structures that facilitate repose, recess, refusal, and reparation in part by redistributing physical and cognitive load from the individual to the institution?

The Inertia Apparatus: Furnishing Repose and Refusal

I regret that I can’t be with you in Basel, and I thank all of you for accommodating me via this virtual apparatus. My telepresence means that I unfortunately haven’t been able to experience, first hand, the intellectual furnishings that have structured your colloquy. [2] As you might know, Margaret Mead and fellow anthropologist / media-maker Paul Byers published, in 1968, a small book in which they explored “those aspects of… the small substantive conference, aimed at the development of ideas and meeting as a single self-contained group around a table. Such a conference is [focused]… on the creation of conditions within which ideas can develop which would not have developed as quickly or at all if the participants had been left to work alone, or in pairs or trios.” She reiterates the central significance of the table: “I shall use the word conference for a group small enough to sit around one large table, called together for a specific purpose, at a specific place,… to consider new aspects of a specified topic.” Mead and Byers found that an event’s physical setting, and particularly the furnishings anchoring it, allow all members to be “visible and audible to all other members with the space between them delimited by a table which formalizes their close and equal relationship.” The table, thus, is an intellectual architecture that models the exchange of language and ideas.

[3] Similarly, Olga Touloumi, in her fantastic book on the design of the United Nations, explains how “tables emerged as the quintessential objects of liberal internationalism”: they “silently installed hierarchies,” determining who gets a seat, whether there’s a head, who sits next to whom, and so forth. [4] The design of the United Nations’ tables — which was given just as much careful consideration as the design of the buildings themselves — “determined the form that the international public sphere would present, and by extension the conversational cultures the organization bestowed on its publics.” Those conversations happened among delegates; between delegates and translators; and between delegates, translators and the press. The physical space and its furnishings had to simultaneously accommodate all levels of exchange.

[5] You might hear echoes of Bruno Latour’s dingpolitic or parliament of things.

[6] Well, one of the reasons I can’t be there with you is that a lot of furniture got in my way — and those very impediments — which are not unique to this particular conference, but which are instead emblematic of broader institutional and epistemological transformations — might give us something to think with. But in order to recognize and analyze the SNAFUS, we also have to acknowledge those systems and apparatae functioning according to plan, typically to facilitate calculation and organization and enhance productivity and efficiency. [7] So, what follows are three sections: first, we’ll look at a range of furnishings, from gadget- to architecture-scale – all of which I’ve explored in my research — and which facilitate intellection or administer intelligence, which are clearly not the same thing.

Then, drawing inspiration from the inertia of the past few years — and the tragicomedies of my own life — we’ll examine a few instances of furniture failure. This little autobiographical preface might seem gratuitous, but it allows me to offer a necessary disclaimer, to explain my absence — and it exemplifies several ways in which furnishings facilitate and frustrate thought; how they order and disorder intelligence. Finally, building on the general vibes of systemic breakdown and infrastructural collapse — and the skepticism, cynicism, and even nihilism they engender — we’ll look at furnishings for repose and refusal as potentially productive tools of restoration and resistance.

[8] THE JUNK DRAWER

[9] For nearly two decades I’ve been mortise-and-tenoning together a research agenda on “case logics” or “intellectual furnishings” — that is: how furniture design shapes our thought and scaffolds our intellectual labor. Drawing a great deal of inspiration from Beatriz Colomina and Lynn Spigel, I’ve written pieces about [10] the architect Louis Kahn’s book carrels, [11] Alvar Aalto’s hexagonal listening stations, and [12] the evolving form of the library service desk. Enjoying commonalities with Markus’s and Craig’s work I’ve written about [13] the histories of the bookshelf and the closet and [14] little artists’ libraries. [15] I worked with a group of industrial designers to create new custom book carts for the Correctional Services team at the New York Public Library. [16] I’ve written about the furnishings and equipment that support off-site storage and underground repositories and the logistics of library circulation. [17] Scaling up from the logics of a single civic system, I looked at the architectures where managers purport to monitor the operations of an entire city or extraterrestrial system.

[18] In 2016, then, I enjoyed a fellowship at the Bauhaus University, which allowed me to catalogue the various logics embedded in different furniture forms. [19] Later on, I wrote about the communal tables that were so prevalent in Silicon Valley work spaces, and which, as I described in a piece for e-flux, created the “material conditions for compulsory community, coercive commitment, and competitive productivity.” [20] In 2018, then, I wrote about the aesthetic and political significance of the various work surfaces at Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation hearing. More recent pieces have focused on [21] the relationships between 19th-century secret drawers (Roentgen desks) and cybersecurity (drawing much inspiration from Carolyn’s wonderful work and echoing Maja’s); [22] and those between architectural containers and memory loss, [23] and the furniture supporting pandemic home-based labor.

[24] Living between NYC and upstate New York generated an interest in the ethics and aesthetics of Shaker architectures, furniture, [25] and apparatae of containment. I know formafantasma designed a spectacular Shaker exhibition, in collaboration with my local Shaker Museum, [26] that was originated at the Vitra Design Museum last summer; I saw it when it moved to Philadelphia this past spring. The Shakers’ principled salesmanship also resonated with [27] my own experience growing up in a hardware store; which I wrote about nearly a decade ago when my family sold our shop. That intersection of organizational aesthetics with material knowledge – which Carolyn discussed so beautifully yesterday – [28] also emerged in my work on toolkits (which Iris has also written about) and cardboard boxes, [29] and the haptic intelligences of sandpaper and repair manuals.

[30] Last spring, I was honored to be the Kluge Chair in Modern Culture at the Library of Congress. After several years of administration and pandemic service, [31] I was eager to use my time at the Library to design conceptual joinery that connected these projects together. But I arrived in Washington, D.C., right before Trump’s inauguration; [32] our orientation activities were infused with an air of dread. And when he entered the White House, [33] the LLM-directed, DOGE-decreed destruction began immediately. I wasn’t sure how I could make furniture relevant or meaningful to this moment. [34] But as I immersed myself in the Library — and other federal and municipal spaces like it around D.C. — I remembered that their intellectual scaffolds, their literal and metaphorical furnishings, [35] are integral to their democratic function. I also came to realize that this administration has a bit of a furniture fetish itself — [36] one that’s both terrifying and hilarious. For a president obsessed with public perception, for a cabinet — here, a convenient pun — defined more by its fabulously shellacked facades and gleaming veneers than by its valuable contents or functioning mechanisms, furniture functions largely as an architectural folly, a prop filling in for the “bureaus” that have historically furnished bureaucracy. [37] So I spent my days with the woodworking and masonry teams, hung out with the Architect of the Capitol, and dedicated my fellowship to [38] a celebration of the bureaus of bureaucracy, [39] and a consideration of how we might deploy “case logics” — imagine rebellious means of organizing information and democracy — to “turn the tables” on this ascendant fascist regime. [40] 

[41] This took me back to some early writing, which I dismissed as fun and frivolous: a counter-reading of a filing manual in which I argued for ludic filing (parallels with Craig’s work on misfiling and Ben Kafka’s work on bureaucratic resistance); [42] and an appreciation of the Zoë Belloff, an experimental filmmaker who turns the Gilbreths’ time-motion studies into slapstick comedy. There was something productively disruptive here.

[43] And that brings us to our second drawer: FURNITURE FAILURE, OR TURNED TABLES

My experience in D.C. was merely one in a series of epiphanically turned tables. I want now to highlight four other spatial vignettes that not only exemplify the inertia that precludes my being with you — but which also prompt broader questions about what kinds of “intelligence” our intellectual furnishings furnish, and how new intelligent agents structure our engagements with the furnished technosocial world.

[44] First: my mom spent 40 years as a special education teacher, which has long attuned me to a capacious understanding of “intelligence.” She retired 12 years ago, and my dad was to follow her a couple years later. But in 2015 she began losing her way in her own neighborhood, finding new threats in her own home. She got lost in her drawers and closets, sorting and re-sorting socks and photos and recipes multiple times each day. Quotidian furnishings became uncanny. I sought to understand the remapping of intelligence that constitutes Alzheimer’s – and I explored the research on how we can furnish a world for our loved ones so they feel as secure and loved as possible even while familiar faces and spatial anchors blur. [44] I wrote a piece about it shortly before we moved my mom into a memory care facility that impressed us with its staff’s humane wisdom. There’s very little that’s rational or data-driven here. It’s all intuitive, patient kindness.

[45] My mom’s condition exemplifies a rapidly growing global phenomenon — one to which most societies are responding with a proliferation of “care” facilities designed by algorithm, smart devices to surveil, chatbots to simulate human engagement, and artificial agents determining who is and isn’t eligible for residential care or hospice. [46] To borrow the title of your research project at Basel, this is assisted thinking for assisted living.

[47] Second: my dad’s a furniture maker. Having owned a hardware store with his brothers, he was intimately familiar with the tools he used. He had deeply informed opinions when I interviewed him for my article about sandpaper. He initially taught himself cabinetry, then began traveling around the country for week-long classes with master craftsmen. You can see on the bottom-left that the secretarire he made for mom exemplifies that tabula that Markus was talking about yesterday. About a year after mom left home, he finally, with our encouragement, gave himself permission to enjoy activities without her – which meant returning to the shop that winter. Yet last November, after an exceptionally dry fall, [48] a wildfire destroyed everything: his shop, multiple generations of tools, irreplaceable equipment, an adjacent barn stuffed with 40,000 board feet of cherry, walnut, tiger and bird’s-eye maple, mahogany, purple heart, and some really stellar pieces of walnut crotch. [49] An insurance algorithm denied the major part of his claim; we see this happening with increasing frequently amidst climate-catalyzed loss of home and furniture. [50] But his own material knowledge — and the fact that he had receipts for every single thing he purchased from his own store — meant that he was able to fight, for 18 months, to secure a sufficient settlement to refurnish his shop, even if the wood itself — procured from friends’ farms and the forest out back — was irreplaceable. Of course not everyone has the wherewithal to fight the algorithm.

[51] Third: let’s dial back a few years before the pandemic. After nearly 20 years on the faculty at The New School in New York, a fancy school began recruiting me for a university professorship – a senior interdisciplinary position. I weighed a few offers, accepted theirs, and, when I showed up on campus in late 2022, learned, much to my surprise, that my service expectations would extend across several academic departments, including many that were in turmoil. Meanwhile, none of those departments remembered to save me an office. [52] So, for my first year, I shared a small office with several emeritus faculty and their stored files and furniture. I was encouraged not to unpack because I’d supposedly be moving soon.

[53] Eight months later, I was transferred to another temporary space in an abandoned hallway with a leaky ceiling in a building a half-mile from my department. There was no WiFi, no administrative support, no mail service (as you can see from the ad hoc pockets folks taped onto their doors), and, obviously, no joy. No furniture either; I had to order it. [54] There was hardly any room for my books and zines and teaching supplies. Yet I did appreciate that there were plenty of built-in filing cabinets, which my predecessor helpfully labeled by writing directly onto the wood fronts. Here we can see his Student Exams drawer – so, if students were to break into his office before finals, they’d know immediately where to find the loot.

I stayed in that temporary space for two more years, while the university burst into flames around me and most of the folks central to my recruitment left. Chain-link fences went up around the college green to prevent student gathering. Quite an inhospitable intellectual furnishing, I must say. It was a calamitous period: everything that could have gone wrong, did. I learned what it meant to inhabit a university that prioritizes wealth accumulation, that regards billionaires’ donations as an end in themselves, [55] and that engages in the unthinking adoption of ed-tech and “success management” software – most of it genAI-powered, and some of it peddled by folks on the board of trustees. [56] A university that proudly pioneered a budget model that positions each program as a stand-alone business in competition with the others. Such a financial model does not facilitate cooperation or resource-sharing… or interdisciplinarity. No communal tables here.

[57] My unfurnished hovel on the margins was emblematic of broader deficiencies in the institution’s organizational culture and data model. And it reminded me that [58] a university is itself multi-scalar intellectual architecture – from its enterprise software interfaces to its course management systems to its budget spreadsheets to its classroom and office arrangements to its campus master plan. [59] We might say that a university administration is rather like a large language model, too, in that it ingests vast bodies of knowledge generated by its faculty and students, and monetizes it, while regurgitating it in official communications as insulting, platitudinous slop.

[60] All of my own intellectual activity was dedicated not to the research questions percolating in my head or through the distributed intelligence of the classroom, but to addressing the dysfunctions of the institution’s intellectual furnishings – or, rather, how its administrative furnishings impede intellection. I hated my job and the fact that I literally had no seat at the table — but if I were to have asked Claude or ChatGPT for advice, it never would’ve advised me to give up a tenured full professorship. People just don’t do that. It would’ve told me to step back, “just say no,” “put my head down” and work. [61] An LLM likely isn’t trained on the testimonials of senior women academics, who, thanks to the pervasive challenges of gendered service expectations, commonly find that “just saying no” just isn’t enough. Yet the kinds of intimate conversations that happened with friends and family around dinner tables – and on my therapist’s couch — ultimately led me to realize that simply “setting boundaries” simply wasn’t possible.

[62] So, last summer I refused. I resigned, loaded up my still-unpacked boxes of books, and left. [63] Those book boxes – including dozens of beautiful art books about furniture that I was initially excited to incorporate into this talk — are unfortunately still boxed up because we’re still waiting for our new house to be inhabitable. That inscrutable mess symbolizes my life at the moment (granted, I’m not subsisting on water and jelly, as was Mikhail Khmyrov, as Michael told us this morning). And my new job, unfortunately, offers little time and few resources for research, as well as limited freedom to travel for my own intellectual pursuits. The new spatiotemporal architecture of my intellectual life requires acclimation.

[64] And before I release you from this confessional digression, I’d like to share one final model of intellectual furnishing: the bed. It was when, for the first time in my life, I landed in a hospital bed two years ago — and was thus freed for one week from the unrelenting demands of academic service, that I was able to reflect on the politics of knowledge that matter to me. [65] That armature of repose scaffolded an intense, sustained reflection on the value of my own intellect, and the ends to which I wanted to put it – not towards repairing a broken institution’s own dysfunctional furniture. I’ve spoken to countless mid-career academic women who’ve had similar experiences: an illness, a prone position, proved revelatory — and liberating — in demonstrating that the body has the capacity to refuse the brain.

[66] And weeks after we escaped from my old university and returned to New York, my partner — a competitive cyclist — found himself in a hospital bed, grappling with the revelation that a 20cm x 20cm tumor was strangulating his heart. At 7am on a Saturday morning, as he lay awaiting a visit from an oncologist, his insurance company called to inform him that they — or, more likely, an AI agent that flagged his file — had determined that his hospitalization and any imminent surgery would not be covered by insurance. So, we packed up, went home, and waited two weeks for the hospital to assemble a team of experts to fight the insurance company — as well as a team of thoracic surgeons, anesthesiologists, and cardiologists within the insurer’s network, who were approved to perform the 12-hour surgery. With that accomplished, my partner was then permitted to occupy a new hospital bed, [67] and then an operating table, and then a chemotherapy chair.

[68] Throughout this excruciating ordeal, during which we were initially advised to prepare for his likely demise, I kept thinking of artist Pepón Osorio’s Convalescence, a magnificent installation I happened upon in the lobby of Jefferson Hospital in Philadelphia. Osorio assembles an array of intellectual furnishings — tables and screens of diagnosis, observation, imaging, invasion, repair, and mourning — as well as media exemplifying the corporeal ontologies and embodied epistemologies each makes possible. “There are five hospital beds, each a tableau of an actual person, unnamed, undergoing treatment for” a variety of ailments. One of those people is Osorio himself, undergoing cancer treatment. [69] The resonant messages here pertain to the power of community care and intelligence, of patients’ self-knowledge, of feelings that don’t make sense, of accepting that life will never be the same.

I ask that you please pardon this confessional, perhaps uncomfortably personal ramble. I share it because these “case studies” have revealed — in life-alteringly profound ways —  how the wisdom unscaffolded by an absent shelf, the material knowledge performed on a clinical table, the steeling self-knowledge incubated in an inaccessible hospital bed, the resolve for resistance erupting from a locked cabinet, are all affective and political. The failures and crises scaffolded by these furnishings also limit what work I can do and what I can share with you today. [70] Yet these aren’t my stories alone: the experiences I described are all merely case studies of broader phenomena — at least in the U.S.: instrumentalized universities, rapacious insurance agencies, insufficient social infrastructures, artificial agents unleashed with the promise of efficiency and impartiality, charged with the authority to target, surveil, interrogate, deport, and deny access to the furnishings of dignity and autonomy and intellectual stimulation.

[71] Now, drawing on what I remember of my still-inaccessible library, I invite you to think with me about [72] furniture that might respond to or resist the institutional failures I described, as well as the dehumanizing, extractive logics of automated intelligences. Can we imagine furnishings for repose and refusal as potentially productive tools of restoration or resistance or refusal? [73] In her study of the Kahnawà:ke Mohawks’ struggle for political sovereignty, anthropologist Audra Simpson theorizes various forms of “refusal”: the refusal to recognize others or to be recognized, the refusal to cede or to retreat when that recognition doesn’t come, the refusal to participate or consent, the refusal to reveal particular privileged knowledge, and so forth. Unlike “resistance,” refusal decenters the state and traditional forms of authority and hierarchy. [74] Sociologist Ruha Benjamin applies Simpson’s work to marginalized populations’ negotiations with biomedicine and commercial technologies, arguing that refusal can’t be reduced to “distrust” or fear; informed refusal is aware of the insufficiency of what’s being offered, and “seeded with a vision of what can and should be.” [75] Tech critic Edward Ongweso speaks specifically to communities’ refusal of generative AI: “Refusal is not just some impotent act of nostalgia, and the extent to which we think so is a measure of our contempt for the prospect of taking democratic politics seriously. We should have a greater role in saying what does and doesn’t get designed or developed or deployed, because we should have a greater role in deciding what sort of politics and what sort of social relations we are party to!”

On May 8, 2026, I presented “Repertoires of Inquiry: Attunement, Curiosity, and Responsibility” at the Bard Center for Curatorial Studies’s Methods Camp.

Repertoires of Inquiry: Attunement, Curiosity, and Responsibility

My career as a researcher began with materials research, although I wouldn’t have known that phrase at the time. [2] My family had a hardware store. Using the materials in that shop, my dad built the two houses in which I grew up, and, starting in a tiny workshop in a corner of the basement in my childhood home, [3] he taught himself woodworking. Over the years, his experiments — [4] with varieties of wood, hand tools, adhesives, finishes, sandpapers — and his engagement with experts — salesmen, customers in the trades and those engaged in various crafts, and, eventually, highly skilled fine woodworker teachers — allowed him to grow into a professional-grade woodworker. [5] He appreciated the challenge of period reproductions; the work wasn’t always my style, but I could certainly appreciate the craft. [6] I still tear up when I open my sock drawer and read the inscription he offered when he made this chest for me 20 years ago.

[7] As he grew, I started off working with the scraps, building pastiched playhouses and lean-tos and rudimentary containers – and often working alongside him to create gifts for friends and, eventually, furnishings for my first apartments. Through those experiments, that play, with materials [8] I learned about physics and math and the importance of sensation — the right angle of light, the touch of woodgrain or sandpaper grit, the distinctive smell of various wood varieties — and about theories of techne and containment and organization. The shop itself was a laboratory — which led me to a different kind of laboratory in college:[9] the chemistry lab. I was good in math and science, and there was limited vocational imagination in my small, rural hometown, so I assumed one put those skills into practice in medicine. Yet my experiments in the lab — with all of its smooth glass test tubes and controlled flames and colored potions — emulsified into the literature seminars I took as an escape from all that logical, test-able thinking.[10] There, I realized that I was equally interested in the stories on the page as I was in the form of its letters and the materiality of the page itself: the translucent onion skin of my Norton anthologies, and the haptics and smell of a small-press letterpress. All of these were part of the meaning, the embodied experience, the sociology of literature and poetry.

[11] I realized in retrospect how lucky I was that my undisciplined curiosities allowed for exposure to different epistemological universes — to realize that, when one beholds book or a painting or a building, there are so many different things to look at and listen to, to smell and to touch, many angles of approach and scales of analysis. So many ways one can ask questions, so many potential tools and frameworks in ones’s research repertoire, provided one stocked it well. [12] Wallace Stevens’s poem, "Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird," became my manifesto.

[13] My dissertation, then, involved coursework across media studies, architectural history, and urban studies, and my dissertation committee included scholars in those three fields. That research combined my interests in texts and their materialization — across scales — by focusing on the design process through which Rem Koolhaas’s Seattle Public Library came into being. This was a provocative design that, in the 1990s and early 2000s, grappled with what a library could be in a rapidly digitizing world, in an increasingly tech-oriented city —  a city famous for its robust public engagement. My research — which was driven by the subject matter and the opportunities that I both sought out, and which were presented to me in the field — encompassed textual analysis of public and institutional records, visual analysis of blueprints and architectural renderings, interviews with librarians and city officials and architects, and participant observation. Again, although I wouldn’t have used the term at the time, I was essentially doing ethnography. I didn’t call it that because I thought such a claim was reserved for trained anthropologists.

[14] I then did a postdoctoral fellowship in art history, and after that, spent 15 years in — and directed programs within — The New School’s media studies department, from which I worked and taught across myriad design fields at Parsons: architecture, urban planning, design and technology, design history, transdisciplinary design. [15] And because much of my research across that decade and a half continued to involve fieldwork, I was eventually recruited to move into anthropology and start a new graduate program in anthropology in design. [16:B] In 2022, then, I was recruited to work across art history and media studies at Penn — but I had also been offered jobs elsewhere in data science, information studies, and design schools. My work across these 20+ years had deployed the methods and approaches to research exemplified in these myriad fields, and I held tenured, full professorships in three of them: anthropology, art history, and media studies.

My exposure to these varied ways of doing research — including, in that anthropology department, what appeared to me a rather precious fetishization of the “ethnographic sensibility,” which you couldn’t teach, but which you were supposed to intuit; and in that art history department, an uncomfortably hagiographic auteur approach to understanding art — [17] made me appreciate all the more the methodological promiscuity in the field — not the discipline, but the field — of media studies. Media studies is a gloriously methodologically promiscuous field: it doesn’t have a defining method or theoretical canon; [18] instead, as I discussed with my colleague McKenzie Wark a few years ago, the object of study — and the context of the research — suggest the appropriate methods.

[19] And knowing what tools and frameworks are right for the job requires having a broad repertoire — including practical skills. Around me, the anthropologists and digital humanists were discovering “multimodal” methods — which recognized that scholarship needn’t be limited to flat textual forms, and that creative practice is an important means of conducting research — but we’d known this all along in media studies. Having a rudimentary knowledge of how your objects of study are made — and understanding the political economy of those production methods — greatly enhances your ability to research it, to analyze it.

[20] I was very fortunate to spend the first two decades of my career in an art-centric institution that, while it offers no resources to support interdisciplinary, exploratory work, at least welcomes it and has used it, for over a century, to reinforce its brand. If I had started my career in the institution where I chose recently to end it — an elite university with boundless, though inequitably distributed and inaccessible, resources; an institution that prioritizes prestige and regards private funding as an index of “quality” — I would’ve been forced into a focused, disciplined trajectory. I would’ve had to become an “expert” in something. [21] Instead, as I realized when I resigned last summer — irreparably alienated by the mismatch between my own research values and the institution’s — [22] I’ve developed expertise not in a subject or a method, but in a sensibility and an ethos. The small, the weird, the local, the public, the principled, and the kind.

[23] These research commitments have been reflected in my choice of research subjects, collaborators, and contexts over the years. I’ve written four books, (co-)edited four collections, and produced multiple student publications about public knowledge, information infrastructures, local media, maps, and maintenance. [24] I’ve also written over 100 articles and book chapters — mostly in open-access venues — about a range of topics — from experimental libraries, geo-archives, deep-time document preservation, lichen typography, olfactory landscapes, and “tree thinking” to local data stewardship, public design processes, pneumatic tubes, sonic interfaces, field guides, repair manuals, and dashboards. [25] Plus lots of about furniture and craft.

[26:B] I’ll highlight just a few projects for which the craft of research might offer some shareable lessons.

On May 5, 2026, I presented “A Convocation of Toolkits” as part of the “Box Things: A Roundtable” at the Peabody Museum at Yale.

A Convocation of Kits: The Formalism of Tools and Methods

The disruptions, losses, and compounding pressures of the pandemic severed supply chains and support networks, upended schedules and traditional divisions of labor. Panic and exhaustion necessitated emergency responses – including plenty of stopgap solutions that minimized cognitive load and maximized efficiency. Kits made it possible to act quickly and confidently, without much headache. [2] The Centers for Disease Control issued a set of toolkits to help build health care workers’ confidence in the COVID-19 vaccine, and to educate patients about its safety and effectiveness.[1] [3] The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, meanwhile, provided vaccine supply kits consisting of syringes, alcohol prep pads, surgical masks, and vaccination record cards.[2] Deluxe models included privacy curtains and cleaning supplies.[3] [4] Meal kits, whose market share was declining immediately before the pandemic, suddenly surged in popularity, rescuing those who lost access to their favorite take-out spots, who were reluctant to roam the supermarket aisles, or who simply couldn’t handle meal prep on top of round-the-clock digital and domestic labor. Even some restaurants found salvation through kits, which allowed loyal customers to recreate their favorite dishes at home.[4] [5] Teachers at all educational levels also turned to kits to deliver a bit of the classroom to students’ bedroom desks and kitchen tables. Several book history and book arts professors worked with Colophon Book Arts Supply to compose class kits – comprising needles and awls and rulers and beeswax and brushes – that their students could purchase for at-home Gutenbergian role-play.[5] [6] And some folks, by then more deeply acquainted with their domestic environments and all their creaks and drafts and leaky faucets, rediscovered the various gadgets that had mysteriously accreted, over decades, at the bottom of their toolboxes.

[7] In the 15th century, "kit" denoted a wooden vessel used to hold water, milk, butter, fish, or some other commodity.[6] That vessel came to hold a much greater variety of things. [8] Since the late 19th century, psychiatrists, psychologists, and a fair share of quack diagnosticians have produced kits crammed with puzzles and dolls and flash cards meant to assess intelligence – particularly that of immigrants, in order to determine their potential value to their new homeland. These various test kits – the “form boards” used by Howard Andrew Knox at Ellis Island, the Stanford-Binet Scales package, the Merrill-Palmer Scale of Mental Tests, the Lowenfeld Mosaic Plates, and the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale kit, to name just a few – are a means of materializing a methodology and an epistemology, one that reifies and objectifies the idea of intelligence as something empirically measurable. [9] And while psychiatrists were boxing up kits to test the capacities of the mind, Johnson & Johnson was packaging sterile surgical supplies into wooden and metal boxes for use by railway workers engaged in hazardous labor far from medical facilities. The company claims to have created the first First Aid Kit in 1888.[7] Today, you can buy “man kits” full of aftershave, razors, and other potions designed to affirm and enhance your virility.

A kit isn’t just a box of supplies; it’s an intentionally and judiciously chosen collection of tools and materials designed to script a particular process, aimed to serve a particular purpose (or purposes, plural), and to do so with minimal waste and frustration. [10] Everything a piecework seamstress needed to embroider a lace collar for a wealthy client, or to darn her children’s socks, was right there in her sewing kit. [11] Everything a soldier might need to mend a torn uniform jacket or affix a new insignia, he’d find right there in his own sewing kit, often called, tellingly, a “housewife,” or hussif.[8] [12] Kits are also sometimes designed to tell a particular story or cultivate a particular identity. Everything a prepper needs to face the apocalypse – a flashlight, a multitool, a hand-crank radio, batteries, matches, water, and so forth – should be right there in his “go bag,” or “bug out bag.”[9] The ideal existential kit would actually be a meta-kit containing other kits, including a first-aid kit and [13] MREs, or Meals Ready-to-Eat.[10] [14] You can also download “Healing Justice Toolkits” and digital literacy toolkits. [15] You can deploy kits to create portable libraries in refugee camps, disaster zones, and underserved urban, rural, and indigenous communities; kits to infuse the methods, style, and ethos of W. E. B. DuBois’s data visualizations more broadly throughout social science and software development; kits to promote participatory development; and kits to attune us to our relations with microorganisms.[11]

[16] But should you? Is a kit really an appropriate means to effect social justice; to teach students about book-binding or physical computing or, heaven forbid, surgery; to engage marginalized communities in designing their material conditions of living? Especially given the proliferation of kits as methodological, epistemological, and political tools in design and development, we need to think about how kits are aesthetic objects that order and arrange things – and how those aesthetics are rhetorical and epistemological. They interpellate particular users and make claims about expertise and whose contributions matter and what knowledge counts. Their component parts shape users’ agency and subjectivity in relation to the objective or purpose at hand – and they have the potential to define that purpose, whether it’s baking a cake or addressing poverty. We need to think about how kits are ontological, too; they constitute a way for tools to be in relation with one another, and for us to be in relation to those tools and to one another, via the toolkit. They also make claims about how the world is put together. We need to consider how kits model particular politics and ethics, what they are well suited to do, and what possibilities are effectively “boxed out.”

[17] Five years ago I published a piece about the aesthetics and epistemology of the toolkit — past, present, and future. In that article I offered a loose typology, starting with [18] kits designed for the most rudimentary of purposes: basic survival. After that: [19] toolkits as means of inclusion and structures of social relations; [20] then toolkits that facilitate material pedagogy; and, finally, [21] toolkitting as a design method. Given the focus of today’s convening — the conceptual box in which we’re all assembled — I’ll skim the first and second categories, spend a bit more time on the third, then explore a few other examples.

[22] TOOLKITS FOR SURVIVAL

  • [23] Prepper kits – aesthetics of knolled survival supplies
  • [24] Kits accompanying soldiers in battle; Red Cross’s 1944 Materia Medica Minimalis list; Doctors without Borders’ toolboxes designed for rapid delivery, simplicity of maintenance; kit as a form of “materialized memory” in crisis settings among a rapidly shifting workforce; kits are a mechanism for distributed cognition — de-localized, globalized, standardized, distilled; kit embodies missing local infrastructure
  • [25] This particular example isn’t explicitly boxy, but it exemplifies the kit as an ethically capacious container: Oakland, CA’s, Collective Kitchen has drawn inspiration from Octavia Butler’s Parable of the Sower, in which the protagonist, Lauren Olamina, facing the loss of her family and community, escapes with a bespoke bug-out bag and a notebook outlining a new world of solidarity — a vision that finds precedent in the Black Panther Party’s survival programs, wherein common protocols and governing doctrines — manifested in a paper bag stuffed with food — can promote widespread solidarity

[26] TOOLKITTING AS A  STRUCTURE OF RELATION

Yet kits are instrumental not only in the deployment of resources or provision of services. They’re not only memory devices, governing apparatae, standardizing formats, and epistemological tools for experts or officials distributing their expertise and skills to others. Kits also serve as means of engagement, as methods of inclusion, as tools of engagement. Given our limited time, I’ll offer just one example:

  • [27] In the 1970s, anti-rape activist Martha “Marty” Goddard took on the standard forensic methods deployed within the Chicago police department, which were based on the presumption that charges of assault were a “feminine delusion” and that male police officers would serve as the voice of the purported victim.  Goddard’s contribution: a [28] kit composed of nail clippers, a comb for collecting hair and fiber, a bag for the victim’s clothing, a card offering her information about support services, test tubes, slides and packaging materials to protect the specimens, sealing tape, a pencil for labeling the slides, and forms for doctors and police officers. Goddard’s rape kit was a cardboard box full of disruptive contradictions: [29] supported by a grant from the Playboy Foundation, branded blue and white by Playboy’s graphic designers, and assembled by a team of senior citizen volunteers at Playboy’s offices, [30] the kit overturned conventions of practice and systems of authority. As Pagan Kennedy describes, Goddard’s low-tech technology “blasted through the assumptions of the day: that nurses were too stupid to collect forensic evidence; that women who ‘cried rape’ were usually lying; and that evidence didn’t really matter when it came to rape, because rape was impossible to prove.”[25] [31] The kit systematized evidence collection and produced a paper trail, which ultimately proved persuasive in the courtroom. The kit was both a scientific tool and a “theatrical prop,” Kennedy notes; it had such charisma, “the kit itself became a character in the trials.”

[32] TOOLKITTING AS MATERIAL PEDAGOGY

As Iris van der Tuin explains, toolkits are particularly useful in interdisciplinary research collaboration; they help to construct a shared language and process – they “externalize and formalize a set of steps,” as we saw with the Doctors Without Borders kits – and thereby cultivate “just enough commonality” to create “conceptual, epistemic, and empirical common ground.”[34] Kits are what Susan Leigh Star and James Griesemer call “boundary objects”: they’re “both plastic enough to adapt local needs and constraints of the several parties employing them, yet robust enough to maintain a common identity across sites.”[35] They’re mediators, translators.

[33] Community Tech New York, an organization committed to digital justice and to building community power through community-owned internet infrastructure, offers [34] “portable network kits,” “a wireless network in a suitcase that helps people [learn] how to build their own mini-internet – and with it, how the internet works and might be owned and governed more equitably.” The kits serve both as a teaching tool and an “emergency standalone wireless network.” The network kits down-scale an intimidatingly, inaccessibly complex infrastructure to make it intelligible and manipulable for common folks. Building their own networks, as CTNY founder Greta Byrum writes, gives communities an opportunity to choose which values they want to instantiate in the infrastructure that binds them together.

  •  [35] I’ll offer, as a brief aside, the Lunchables kit, or the cake mix, as a “kit” of domestic empowerment — which we can contrast with [36] the Japanese lunchbox. Kenji Ekuan describes how the lunchbox offers a much richer pedagogical experience: it embodies beauty of form, functional multiplicity, unification in diversity, ultimate adaptability, and generosity – and it’s an object lesson in waste-avoidance. It demonstrates how equipment – the box with its multiple partitions – can “excite creativity.”

[37] Boxes can be portals to a worldly, sensory education. In the early 19th century clergyman and professor Charles Mayo traveled to Switzerland to study with education reformer Johann Pestalozzi, who advocated for children’s embodied engagement with their material environments. He returned to London and established a school outside of the city. [38] His sister, Elizabeth, published a book to support the school’s curriculum: Lessons on Objects offered 100 lessons on 100 objects. As Ann-Sophie Lehmann explains, the curriculum was built on the assumption that “the qualities of materials should first be experienced before they are defined with specific terms. The book fails to mention exactly how those materials are to be procured – but an advertisement at the back of the book notes that “cabinets, containing the substances referred to in these lessons” can be purchased at various shops. [39] Those mahogany boxes, Lehmann writes, “are extraordinarily beautiful in the way they hold the material universe, [40] stacked neatly in four trays.” Unlike wunderkammern, which display the rare and curious, these boxes catalogue the quotidian. Lehmann describes one of the four extant boxes: [41] “In the lower left corner, we encounter the quill, the pencil and the ladybug, which together serve to embody the profound contrast between nature and artifice, life and death. Only the flower is missing. We can assume that it would have been plucked directly from nature for this purpose, just like milk and an egg are present in the book but not in the box.” And another: this “stuff was used, broken, and lost, and teachers needed to replace and thereby expand the repertoire of the Mayos.” These wooden boxes contained pieces of a world that students were encouraged to scrutinize and fondle and sniff, with the hope that such engagement would prompt a similar sensory engagement with the broader world beyond the kit and the classroom and the school building that contained it.

[42] What of the Bell Labs science kits,  [43] or Berkeley Enterprises’ Brainiac Kits,  [44] or the Center for Urban Pedagogy’s kits for teaching about complex urban systems? [45] Or the fetishized kits of aestheticized data collection I wrote about back in 2013? They evidenced researchers’ fascination with the sensory, affective, subjective dimensions of measuring things. To feed their passion, they designed a host of measurement tools as objets d’art: lovely little bento boxes of tools, fanciful surveying equipment.

[46] What of Flux kits and [47] method decks and [48] this 19th-century Studley tool cabinet [CLICK] or this lady toolbox – [49] or ToolboxToolbox which is, as its name implies, a kit of kits attesting to the proliferation of “toolboxes” to solve problems and address challenges ranging from remote work to venture design to racism and decolonization.[61] Can all such “problems” be solved with a kit-of-parts methodology?

[50] Perhaps these assemblages of tools, these methodological bento boxes, can be like the Japanese lunchbox in that they invite us to reflect upon the delights inside – the forms and affordances of each tool, and the discipline each requires. Seeing those tools in relation to each other, we can inquire about the multiple adaptive functions they might serve, how they complement one another, how they can cultivate generosity. And perhaps the boxes themselves — in their dimension and materiality and aesthetics — can offer new ethical and pedagogical frames, reshaping the contexts for tool use, and informing the worlds we build with them. [51]

How to Conduct an Didactic Dismantlement:
A Catalogue of Pedagogic Deeds

I was delighted to receive an invitation from Irina and Sonali last fall to join you this semester — largely because I found the theme of this series, [2] Pedagogy of the Deed, so compelling. I’ll admit that I have a fraught relationship with Columbia. Of course everyone has a fraught relationship with Columbia these days, amidst so much institutional malice and cowardice — but my unease runs deep. I’ve shared a few hundred invited talks across my quarter-century in the academy, but I’ve rarely felt so unsure of myself, even as a senior scholar, as I have when I’ve presented my work at Columbia. It was here where I, as an NYU graduate student, first mustered up the courage to ask a question at a public event, only to receive such a dismissive response from the all-senior-male panel that I didn’t speak up again in public events for a long while. And in the decades that followed: aside from many lovely conversations at GSAPP, I found that I simply don’t make sense here. Columbia and I seem to be on different wavelengths. But this particular theme spoke to my current preoccupations., so I’m hoping we mind find some synergy.

On one of my more recent visits to your neighborhood, [3] I was set to talk about pedagogy at the Barnard Center for Engaged Pedagogy in late 2023. But the night before my talk, on the second day of a two-day symposium, I suffered a strangulated hernia — or, more specifically,  [4] an internal herniation of the Meckel’s diverticulum through the foramen of Winslow, a magnificent-sounding and crazy-rare condition with a >50% mortality rate. [5] I survived, obviously. But by the time I recuperated and we rescheduled, both uptown campuses had erupted into chaos and carcerality,  [6] so the Barnard team accommodated my request to move our event to a venue whose vibe better fit my values: the Prime Produce Apprentice Cooperative in Hells Kitchen.

[7] At the time, I had recently moved — after nearly two decades at The New School — to an endowed university professorship at Penn, a position for which I had been recruited for several years, and which I had chosen from among several offers. [8] Yet the hernia proved to be a portent for deep discomfort to come, a synecdoche for that whole tragicomic chapter of my life — one that included not only Alzheimer’s and cancer and fire and copyright trolls and, at this very moment, more cancer, but also, on the institutional front, hilarious and heartbreaking disappointment and liberating disillusionment.

[9] Penn’s campus, like yours, descended into chaos, albeit chaos of a less spectacular variety. Its administration proved just as cowardly as Columbia’s, although less loudly so. [10] Penn has recently drawn measured praise for refusing to hand over a “list of Jews” to the federal government, but three years ago they readily shared the names, contact information, syllabi, and email archives of faculty involved in campus activism. Most of the people central to my recruitment departed shortly after my arrival, dysfunction reigned, [11] money ruled, rich donors dictated policy, and I grew confused, angry, appalled, and embarrassed by the spineless deeds and toothless rhetoric of that storied institution, where pedagogy seemed to serve largely as a means to manufacture prestige and perpetuate private equity. [12] Administrators evoked the Franklinian legacy at every turn while churning out hedge funders bent on destroying the institutions and values that Franklin championed.

[13] Amidst all of this, I wrote two cathartic blog posts about my self-education — both my andragogical (adult teaching) and heutagogical (self-directed learning) experiences — and how it led me to particular deeds of self-preservation. The first missive came when I realized that my fancy job made me absolutely miserable and simply could not provide the conditions for me to do the work I had ostensibly been recruited to do. I recognized that all the “good deeds” required in academia’s volunteer economy, the calling to service that’s so often inescapable to mid-career women, proved untenable. I required the rogue deeds of my own body — causing intense pain in order to provoke an epiphany— to teach me that simply “saying no,” repeatedly practicing refusal, was pathetically inadequate to handle deeper, systemic dysfunctions — gendered and racialized and classed — in this industry. I refused refusal as a coping strategy — then put in another semester of 90-hour work weeks, managing turmoil and transition across three programs, without a dedicated faculty office.

[14] I posted another missive in June 2025 as I submitted my resignation, one day before Penn agreed to recognize the existence of only two genders. [15] While the first post addressed the individual consequences of institutional dysfunction, the second homed in the glaring mismatch between this institution’s professed beliefs and its actions, its mission and its deeds, its values and mine. As the then-new Trump administration launched repeated and amplified attacks on higher education, I wrote:

[16] I remember attending a Spring 2025 campus event addressing those very threats. Penn’s university president — the one installed after Liz Magill was scapegoated, then ousted, by the institution’s own board — initiated the panel discussion by acknowledging how important it is “that we lead with our values.” So, Penn, founded in 1740, “recently created a values statement.” Recently. Benefiting from multiple centuries’ hindsight, steeled by the threat of existential risk, the institution affirmed its commitment to excellence, respect, brilliance, being inventive, and “recruiting the most talented individuals.”

Institutional values and mission statements, of course, are meant to be pedagogical. Yet….

I’d argue that these aren’t “values”: they’re an AI-generated platitudinous self-help meme. These are the “values” you tack up in the staff break room at Salesforce — not the bold, ethical principles that anchor an institution whose contributions are vital to our social, environmental, and political welfare. An institution currently under attack from a fascistic, anti-intellectual, truth-warping regime. A regime “trained” and legitimated by our very own “elite” institutions. Our values should reflect reconciliation with these facts.

[17] These anodyne “values” might infuse classroom discourse, but their operationalization — through curriculum design, campus clubs, job fairs, networking events, and other “extra-curricular” outlets — demonstrate the potent and potentially poisonous pedagogy of the deed. [18] Students covet their classmates’ Wall Street and McKinsey internships and sophomore-year job offers, and they behold the conveniently elastic, polysemic nature of the institution’s pedagogical principles in practice in these contexts. Yet a pedagogy based in platitudes doesn’t merely lend itself to capitalist capture.

[19] Such milquetoast mores also lend themselves to authoritarian co-optation. The White House — recently commandeered by a few Penn grads — can claim to be hiring “the best,” “most talented,” “meritorious” individuals who display utmost “respect” for and loyalty to the Supreme Leader, who are committed to American “excellence” and engaged in “inventive” reinterpretations of the Constitution. When I look at Donald Trump, Don Jr., Elon Musk, Kevin Hassett, Dr. Oz, and their ilk, I don’t (entirely?) blame Penn — but I do see in these alums the dangers of an instrumentalist, entrepreneurial education. I see what happens when you build a university around a business school, and then run a nation like a business; when education cultivates cunning that’s deployed for the purposes of deception and extraction. When I watch these men proudly perform their ignorance and egotism and fraudulence on screen, I’m embarrassed, appalled, and furious.

[20] Penn might be a particularly prolific generator of such figures, but it’s certainly not alone. So many elite institutions share a repertoire of aspirational deeds that serve a pedagogical purpose: in a culture in which even the federal government equates starting salary with educational value, these markers of success exemplify what’s rewarded, and they draw recruits who want to reap those rewards. It’s a self-perpetuating culture.

Yet pedagogical deeds needn’t be as grand and destructive as nurturing 1000 hedge funds or producing military technology. [21] Pedagogy also becomes practice, or deed, through bureaucratic and technical choices made at a seemingly far remove from the noble work of the classroom. Even the choice of enterprise software, the selection of board members, the choice of budgeting models, the prioritization of particular capital projects and the selection of architects: all are deeds that engineer the substructure of pedagogy. And all are matters that, if higher education is to be salvaged and reimagined, we have to understand.

[22] There’s been widespread critique of universities’ uncritical adoption of and curricular imperatives around AI — but even an institution’s choice of course management system is itself a deed that shapes the realm of pedagogical possibility, and transforms the learning experience into a series of technologically mediated and surveilled transactions. [23] Many years ago one of my former dissertation advisees, Jeffrey Moro, wrote a widely circulated post about why he refused to use ed-tech platforms that infused “cop shit” into the classroom, cultivating an ambiance of distrust. [24] Literary scholar Matt Seybold, whose podcasts have become a forum for critical university studies, is now exploring the corporate history and political economy of the course management system Canvas, which was purchased in 2024 by a private equity form and is now teeming with AI features. [24] I’d also like to call your attention to more mundane technologies that are not unique to universities, but which shape their conditions of labor: [25] Consider WorkDay, which contributes to the responsibilization of faculty and students as department-level support-staff dwindle, and as adjunct pools and administrative teams grow. As noted in a shockingly astute 2024 Business Insider article — truly, a model of software hermeneutics — Matt Alston notes that WorkDay exists to distribute work and collect data. WorkDay isn’t an “ed-tech” product, but it still necessitates deeds that have a pedagogical purpose; it enacts a value system through its data model and workflow.

[26] Consider also the university board, of which, I imagine, very few students are aware. Very few faculty paid attention to their boards until recently – to our detriment.

  • Penn GIDEST anecdote
  • Serving on executive-level search committee during my first year at Penn; researched all board members – all in finance, consulting, real estate development and biotech
    • All finance buildings and labs and resources – and all drive curriculum

[27] The past three years revealed the dangers of Wall Street overrepresentation on university boards.

[28] Avoiding these risks and limitations was one of the founding motivations for a group of Columbia defectors to found The New School in 1919. [READ SLIDE] [29] I recently had occasion to visit The New School’s origins — its recognition that the design of curricula and governance structures and civic partnerships are deeds with profound pedagogical significance for all who work and study there. I was honored to be invited to keynote the graduate student conference in my old department on the occasion of both the department’s 50th anniversary and the revival of the conference after a 10-year hiatus. The administration’s choice to pause the program, and focus primarily on media screenings, was a deed that deleteriously shaped department culture and limited students’ understanding of what counts as media studies, and what work is worthy of public exhibition and celebration. [30] The revival of the conference coincided with the resuscitation of a student newsletter and other programs — just as all my faculty colleagues received voluntary separation letters and the institution threatened 15% faculty cuts.

[31] In preparing that talk a month ago, I was able to appreciate the prescience and timelessness of the school’s founders’ concerns and commitments — including minimizing the intrusion of business principles, a phenomenon that faculty member Thorstein Veblen had critiqued in years prior. [32] Instead, teachers and researchers would be “emancipated” from their “obligations to donors, trustees and university management,” and freed to “know their own strength and weakness.” [33] Of course these appealing principles had to be operationalized through various management decisions — including the refusal to establish a substantial endowment, which precipitated financial precarity that has plagued the institution ever since. Yet as my friend and colleague Julia Foulkes noted, the model quickly proved impracticable. She writes: “As the founding faculty abandoned the rudderless school over its first three years, a Director superseded the Organizing Committee. From that time to nearly the end of the 20th century, a small team of administrators was the true backbone.” That director, Alvin Johnson, would create courses in quick time to respond to current events and social needs; find experts to teach them; and promote those courses to a changing, non-degree-seeking roster of students. The part-time faculty didn’t expect continual employment. The institution’s values-driven preference for nimbleness and responsiveness — both pedagogical concerns — and frugality ultimately necessitated contingency. TNS, Foulks writes, had long “come to depend on the frank exploitation of part-time labor… to support its values of academic freedom” in its more prestigious division. [34] In this regard, The New School was prescient, prefigurative of contemporary laments in higher education: a century ago, it did the deed of intentionally choosing the contingent labor model that has weakened so many other universities, and compromised the conditions of teaching and learning, at countless other schools across the country.

[35] Unlike Penn, to which I felt absolutely no affinity from the moment I stepped on campus and its soullessness became palpably apparent, I have a great fondness for The New School in all its complicated, hypocritical imperfections. Its founding values, when activated through operational deeds, may have proven unsustainable – but that mission has indeed drawn a thrillingly vibrant community: the most exciting pedagogical environment. And it’s now at risk. Drawing inspiration from Shirley Chisholm, I so deeply value its ideas, its promise — the need for the kind of pedagogy that it [36] and similar institutions, like Hampshire College, espouse, if not always practice — that I feel compelled to critique it.

[37] Which brings me back to the promise of this very series: the Pedagogy of the Deed.

  • Appreciate focus on deeds because that’s all I’ve had time for over the past few years, as institutional turmoil and personal challenges sidelined my research.
  • [38] I appreciate that it centers pedagogy — which I’ve always regarded as a critical part of my identity as a scholar, and as a scholarly practice in its own right
  • Syllabi as scholarly documents – a great way to frame principles as “deeds”
  • [39] I’ve designed over 40 classes and, since 2002, built open-access public websites for nearly all of them, “commoned” my teaching resources and shared – with their permission – my students’ work. Those websites were meant to model an intellectual conviviality and generosity that then infused the classroom.
    • I’ve also sought to align those pedagogical values with, and model them through, my own research – all about public knowledge resources and open access

[40] Last class I taught at TNS, in 2022: Redesigning the Academy — exemplified the pedagogy of the deed

[41] Designed to foster constructive critique and imagining otherwise

  • [45] Wanted to demo for students that values – and creative and ethical possibilities – infuse all phases of research: from choice of topic, to the net one casts for a literature review, to choice of empirical methods or critical evaluative methods, to choice of mode of presentation and distribution, etc.

[51-7] METRO

As you can probably tell — and I apologize for the gratuitous, cathartic self-referentiality of it all — I had quite an earth-shattering pedagogical experience over the past few years, which compelled me to perform some pretty radical deeds: I left the academy and gave up tenure. But I did so not in a futile act of refusal, but in order to catalogue and recapture those pedagogical values that define me, and which I can transform into intentional deeds in more convivial contexts. [58] As I wrote in my resignation post 10 months ago: “I’m good at this job. Rather, I was good at this job — and I’ll become so again in an environment whose values align with those that animate my work: the small, the weird, the local, the public, the principled, and, whenever possible, the kind.”

Now, I’m not sure if such values are incompatible with a place like Columbia — but I certainly found them impossible amidst the converging crises I arrived into at Penn. And I was so profoundly disappointed by a academia – by an institution that embodied its worst inclinations, at least when I was there — that I couldn’t fathom starting over again. Hence my detour.

[59] But I’m eager now to turn away from my own case study and use our remaining time to reflect on your environment — not in the form of a lecture, with me telling you what I think, but rather, in keeping with the spirit of the series theme, in the form of a seminar. [60] If you read my abstract for this event, you might recall that I had proposed that we collectively create a Diagram of Defiant Deeds for Pedagogical Probity. I imagined this being a collaborative project with a graphic designer, which would yield a zine you’d all take home. But the continual calamities and chemotherapy that transpired between abstract submission and today precluded that well-intentional exercise from taking shape.

Instead, we’ll consider: [61-2] Who are the various stakeholders, or deed-doers, in this ongoing didactic dismantlement? What forms of sabotage or resistance, acquiescence or agitation do they perform? And what is the pedagogical – or androgogical, or auto-didactic — import of those deeds? I encourage us to think capaciously about the entire Foucauldian apparatus — beyond the usual suspects, toward the minor characters, and even beyond human agents toward the work that policies and platforms do.

[63] Consider the government antagonists, the saboteur trustees, the acquiescent administrators, the firebrand educators, the acquiescent compliance officers, the impassioned (or not) students (and student journalists), the “security” officers and their surveillance cameras, the “free-speech” agitators, the ed-tech tricksters, the AI hucksters and their voracious bots. All enact various deeds, sometimes in response or opposition to each other, and all — however automatic or unthinking through they seem — reveal a theory of pedagogy and democracy.

When are the students teaching the teachers? When are the designated pedagogues inadvertently teaching lessons about how not to be? What does a reified convention or a technical limitation teach us through its naturalization?
