Pointing at Clouds: Indexing, Searching, and Citing in an Age of AI Smog

[2] It’s been a cold, cloudy winter, after a year of diminishing hope. Our institutional futures are foggy. [3] The federal government has both incentivized the generation of more greenhouse gases and precluded aerial means of mitigation. [4] More and more people are coming to realize that “the cloud" was a gauzy euphemism for [5] an extractive, nefarious global apparatus that devours natural resources, [6] while tracking, entrapping, and annihilating people in our own communities and around the world. [7] The same artificial agents many folks rely upon to churn out pro forma emails and term papers, the same databases many legal and tax scholars consult for current research: they’re also empowering militaries to target civilians from Minneapolis to Tehran, generating clouds of terror and trauma. [8] Media scholar Yuriko Furuhata explains how even the work of classifying cloud types risks a sort of epistemic violence: she compares two Cold War-era cloud atlases and finds that the Japanese text includes mushroom clouds as a species, while the American atlas does not — which makes me wonder if we should start classifying data centers as a sort of invasive nimbostratus sub-species, too.[i]

Perhaps strategically deployed by OpenAI-powered geolocation technologies, [9] a cloud has certainly decided to park above me for the past few years — and it’s enveloped those I love. [10] As Alzheimer’s has been progressively clouding my mom’s memory for over a decade, a cloud of fire and smoke consumed my professional woodworker dad’s entire woodshop and supply barn last year. [11] And just two months ago, an X-ray revealed a cloud that enshrouded my partner’s lung and heart. He miraculously survived a surgery that profoundly obfuscated our future, and he’ll start his third chemotherapy infusion before we leave here this afternoon.

[12] Speaking of conflagrations and metastasis, some of you might also know that, just a few months ago, I left a nearly quarter-century faculty career – most recently, an endowed presidential professorship — because of utter burnout and seemingly inescapable gendered service disparities and terminal disillusionment with elite higher education’s profound ethical miasma. As someone who has long studied public knowledge and media infrastructures, and who’s collaborated with New York’s libraries and archives, I had become painfully aware that my values and those defining elite higher education — [13] which imagines itself floating among the cirrostratus, and assumes that its value derives from that altitude — had diverged. I was naively shocked to find myself serving on committees with alums and trustees who were patent flippers and hedge funders — leaders of the very industries effecting slow violence against public knowledge. Ingratiating oneself and pursuing “named gift opportunities” with these folks — ethical integrity be damned — was a metric of success. I was incredibly annoyed to watch a leading research library celebrate its first-ever massive open-access partnership… with Elsevier. I was perplexed to see leading scholars publish radically progressive books with imprints under the Murdoch empire. The aura of eminence — the perfume of supremacy — seemed so frequently to divert folks’ capacity to point out the inequities and hypocrisies behind all the smoke and mirrors.

[14] So, I inventoried my own work and indexed it against what the institution had become, and — through a period of dark and storm introspection — decided it was time to depart. [15] Now I have a new role with an institution founded by the state in 1964 to promote the sharing of research and reference resources across all the libraries and archives in NYC and Westchester County. [16] I had served on the board of the Metro NY Library Council for ten years, but now I’m its Director of Creative Research, which involves [17] helping to imagine a new, experimental outdoor library, for which we just acquired 26 verdant acres in Westchester. I’m also charged with developing research projects that bridge the city’s public knowledge resources, and launching [18] new, exuberantly interdisciplinary public classes that cross-reference the city’s knowledge institutions. In the fall we celebrated misfits, and this spring we’re reinvigorating search and discovery.

Because much of my work now involves a form of creative indexing, I was particularly heartened to receive — just as I was mapping out my resignation from the academy — [19] an invitation to serve as the 2025 Design Indexer in Residence at the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum. [20] I’m very grateful to curators Alexandra Hodkowski and Alexa Griffith, and librarians Jennifer Bracchi, Flannery Cusick, and Michelle Jackson-Beckett for hosting me and making my stay such a generative and friendly experience — even while institutional tumult and pervasive attacks on federal workers clouded their day-to-day work experiences and long-term plans.

[21] A Design Index residency seemed to offer an ideal opportunity take stock — to peer through the fog and find some stabilizing order. [22] Over the preceding two decades, I’d written about libraries and databases and interface aesthetics and bookshelves and manuals and toolkits and bookmarking platforms and lists and headstone typography and index cards, [23] so I was delighted to have the opportunity to explore the index in all its prismatic capaciousness — and to invite my [24] friend Kelli Anderson, artist book maker and paper engineer extraordinaire, to join me.

[25] I wanted to show how an index is not just a bibliographic convention, or an organizational method, or a media form, or a financial instrument, or a corporeal component; it’s also an intellectual architecture, a literary genre, a creative form, a semiotic concept, and an embodiment of agency — one that might offer an important antidote to the pervasive autonomous, extractive cloudification of our contemporary information ecology. [26] Henry Wheatley — president of the Samuel Pepys Club, vice president of the Bibliographical Society, and assistant secretary to the Royal Society of the Arts — proposed a similarly capacious conception in his 1878 “What Is an Index?” An index, he says, is an “indicator or pointer-out of the position of required information, such as the finger-post on a high road, or the index finger of the human hand.”[ii]

Since Wheatley’s time, the index has of course been transformed by technological, sociological, and political change. [27] Let’s jump ahead a century. [28] When it was born in 1994, Yahoo! was indexed by human beings — professional, specialized web surfers. [29] Today Google’s bots crawl the web; analyze each page’s text, content tags, images, and videos; and store all that information in a large database — an index — which is actually what we’re searching when we Google something.[iii] [30] Of course now with artificial intelligence-infused search, [31] we lose the capacity to point toward — to index — the sources from which our results are drawn, and to assess their veracity and credibility. [32] Those book-length sources — that is, if they’re written by humans (which, these days, is not a given) — are themselves still typically indexed by professional book indexers who, while perhaps aided by digital tools, still practice a human art.[iv]

[33] Next week, in my Search & Discovery class, we’re visiting Google — as an ethnographic exercise — to talk about the devolution of web search, and to contrast different genealogies of digital discovery: commercial search engines, library discovery tools, and speculative, activist, and poetic methods of exploration. We’ll be joined by folks from Google Search; the NYPL’s manager of metadata services, Karly Wildenhaus; and critical technologist Sam Lavigne. Going to Google — its physical campus, not the website — allows us to visit a node in the cloud, to point to the people who make the decisions that shape institutions and create path dependencies. [34] For a couple decades I’ve been writing about, and teaching classes that demonstrate, the value of embodied experiences of obfuscatory infrastructures: touching the cloud, indexing the AI supply chain. [35] Lots of others are doing this work, too: Lisa Parks, Nicole Starosielski, Sarah Roberts, Mél Hogan, Ingrid Burrington, Kate Crawford, Vladan Joler, Zane Cooper, Sarah Lamdan, and the Estampa collective, who made this fantastic map of generative AI. Next week, we’ll get a better sense of why our indices of global knowledge are deteriorating.

[36] Digital technology has also transformed our manual means of textual engagement: on paper, the index finger turns pages; on the screen, it clicks and scrolls and joins with the thumb to pinch and zoom. [37] As an aside, I’ll note that, several years ago, I shared a talk about the history of the mousepad that I never had an opportunity to share again! [38] The capacity, or compulsion, to click has changed the nature of our social and political engagement: it’s how we register our approvals and allegiances, our resentments and rejections. [39] It’s also how the current regime performs the pageantry of governance.

[40] The same obfuscation that characterizes artificial intelligence — to whom or what do we point for authority and accountability — characterizes our political realm. This Kevin Kallaugher cartoon evokes the classic deflection of responsibility, [41] but with the preponderance of “distraction” as a political strategy (or scapegoat), [42] as well as the proliferation of AI slop and misinformation — which, notably, has historically given itself away through its mangling of the fingers — it’s hard to know where to point… for credit or blame. [43] DOGE created massive indexes, or concordances, of verboten key terms — diversity, citizenship, gender, tribal, climate — and fed them in to ChatGPT to execute blanket deletions. [44] The chaotic state of our political affairs has led some activists to create their own indexes of destruction and resistance.

[45] Meanwhile, the reification and prioritization of particular financial indexes — that is, a group of assets that represents a specific market — has distorted our understanding of the economy and dangerously inflated the AI industry’s role in it. Michael Burry, of Big Short fame, recommends this explainer in the AI/End of the World newsletter: “This AI-fuelled [price-to-earnings] premium feels like betting the farm on a future where automation wins big. But if automation wins, it wins by replacing the people whose spending powers the economy. And if it doesn’t win, we’ve allocated hundreds of billions in capital to infrastructure that doesn’t generate returns, financed by circular investments and record debt. Either way, the structure is unstable.”[v]

[46] This is the increasingly cloudy context toward which I aimed to… well, perhaps not point, but, rather, gesticulate wildly as I reassessed the conditions and possibilities of the index. [47] At the Cooper Hewitt Library, I spent three months exploring the closed stacks to index various manifestations of indices, and I organized them into three sets of typological units, spread across three tables.

[48] We began at Table #1 with [49] the most “textbook,” or conventionally bibliographic, conceptions of the term. [50] We drew here from Dennis Duncan’s 2022 book, Index, A History of the. In the index of Duncan’s book we can find one Richard Collison, who proposed that “When a housewife makes a separate place for everything in the kitchen she is in fact creating a living index, for not only she, but all her household, will gradually get used to the system she has created and be able to discover things for themselves.”[vi] [CLICK] We might thus regard the tables in this room as a living index of my own intellectual organization of the Cooper Hewitt’s library collection. This is merely a microcosmic manifestation of the larger concern of architectural determinism: how the physical spaces of the library and its furnishings play a role in determining how collections are constructed and arranged, and how knowledge is made from them. More about this later.

Duncan tells us that the index “is an invention of the codex era, and not the age of the scroll. It is a truly random-access technology, and as such it relies on the form of the book that can be opened with as much ease in the middle, or at the end, as at the beginning. The codex is the medium in which the index first makes sense.”[vii] And the culture surrounding the codex — particularly, new universities and religious institutions where teaching and preaching favored “external demonstration over inner revelation,” and which trafficked in the genres of the lecture and the sermon — required “new tools on the page, new ways of efficiently finding parcels of text.”[viii]

Here, we see here a variety of books opened to random pages, to which an index directed us. I’d argue that these particular indexes also point us toward things beyond their pages — outside this room, even.

[51] Consider first the New York Directory and Register (1789). A directory. [52] Wheatley informs us that for much of history, the term “index” was used interchangeably with table, register, calendar, summary, and syllabus. [53] I’d argue that this directory — an “alphabetical list of the Names, Occupations, and Places of Abode of the Citizens of New York” — also functions as a historical index to, it points outward to, the craftspeople and creative geographies of the city. We learn where merchants, hardware and cordage shopkeepers, blacksmiths, shipwrights, shoe makers, hair dressers, carpenters, coopers, goldsmiths, wheelwrights, and milliners, live and work (14).

[54] The “Index of Architecturally Notable Structures in Greater New York” at the back of Alan Burnham’s New York Landmarks (1963) trains our observation of the city differently (355+). We’re prompted to look at a building’s structure, architect, and style, and whether it exemplifies a particular urban feature: Does it have stained glass, iron, or other metalwork, mosaics or murals? Is there sculpture incorporated into the facade? Is it of historical interest? Does it represent a feat of landscaping and civic planning? In a sense, Burnham’s index exemplifies Duncan’s distinction between, on the one hand, a word index — that is, a concordance that simply lists which words are used and where — and, on the other hand, a subject index, which requires some analysis and abstraction. Burnham extrapolates beyond the fact of the image to catalogue the broader urban significance those images document.

[55] E. Winifred Alt’s Index to Handicrafts, Model Making, and Workshop Projects (1969) doesn’t so much index the city, but the myriad crafts it might contain: from adhesives to basketmaking to clothespins to hinges to sconces and umbrella stands and zoetropes. They also clarify what doesn’t count: “Electronic devices are included, but not radio and television technology; construction of photographic equipment, but not its use; specific needlework items such as purses, hats, bags, but not basic sewing, embroidery or kitting instructions. Cookery and gardening continue to be omitted.” This is itself an index of absences.

[56] Laurence Urdang and Frank Abate, eds., Fine and Applied Arts Terms Index (1983) further helps us build a vocabulary. The authors have “selected terms for inclusion… from more than 150 sources: dictionaries and encyclopedias, auction catalogues, periodicals, and other published materials have been culled for words and phrases dealing with every period and style of fine and applied art” (8). Theirs, they say, is “the first major attempt at systematic documentation of a field that is extremely productive and imaginative in its coinages and borrowings.” The index tames this linguistic tangle.

[57] I also included a contemporary index – Mindy Seu’s Cyberfeminism Index — which, in exhaustively cataloguing global genealogies of feminist thought about technology, reminds us of the myriad ways we could have avoided the technofascist present Silicon Valley’s techbros have created for us. An index of the otherwise.

[58] The Builder: Illustrations Index, 1843-1883, compiled in 1994, lists, in textual format, the subjects, illustrators, engravers, and other information represented in the copious illustrations in this weekly architecture magazine across four decades of the 19th century. The editors note that “the illustrations are a delight in themselves, but it is the information they convey, here unlocked for the first time, that will surely be most appreciated by this volume’s many users.” Exemplifying visual literacy, these indexers index what the untrained eye can’t see. [59] Meanwhile, Barbara Suit Janssen, in the Smithsonian Patent Models Index: Guide to the Collections of the National Museum of American History, Smithsonian Institution (1980), recognizes that, like the Builder’s illustrations, the often-intricate models that accompanied nineteenth-century patent applications contain a great deal of information about craft and culture and engineering and economics— if we can extrapolate from the indexed list itself.

This recognition that material objects — and not just the words locked on a page — are worthy of indexing, defines [60] the next work, the Index of American Design (1950), which I assumed was the namesake of the Design Index residency, but I learned that it’s not! Regardless, it warrants some attention because of both what it is — and what it says about federal cultural agencies in an age when they’re facing countless challenges. We might look at the Index of American Design as a project-scaled index of, a material manifestation of, the robustness of government support for public culture. It’s like the Dow Jones for federal art and design investment.

[61] The project was the brainchild of painter and textile designer Ruth Reeves and Romana Javitz, a librarian at the New York Public Library and steward of its legendary Picture Collection from 1929 to 1968 ([62] I want to briefly acknowledge Diana Kamin’s fantastic book that engages with Javitz and other picture collections). [63] Reeves and Javitz shared a frustration with their inability to find images of American craft, which, as Edwin Christensen writes in this volume, was attracting greater attention in American cultural heritage institutions.[ix] Reeves and Javitz pitched their visual resource to Frances Pollack, who ran educational programs at New York’s Emergency Relief Administration.[x] The pilot project’s success then yielded an invitation — back when such things were possible! — to scale up nationally through the Federal Art Project in the Works Progress Administration. From 1935 to 1939 project staff commissioned over 18,000 watercolors from over 1,000 out-of-work artists in 34 states and Washington, D.C. They paid their creators, unlike the artificially-intelligent “indexers” at today’s generative AI companies, for whom “indexing” is merely ingesting content.

[64] The Index of American Design’s state directors were instructed to prioritize historically significant but under-studied and endangered material, as well as regional and local crafts. They requested paintings of “weathervanes, knives, mantel clocks, bonnets, cradles, ship figureheads, cake molds, and wedding corsets.”[xi] Within the collection were many textiles: quilts, embroideries, samplers. We also find egg beaters, tavern signs, butter molds, and puppets. The New York office contributed over 5000 renderings, including a rich collection of costumes. I’m particularly taken by the poetic groupings we see in the book: “Bird and Tulip,” featuring Pennsylvania Dutch craft, “Work and Faith,” featuring Shaker craft, “Saints and Saddles,” featuring Southwestern indigenous craft, as well as other sections on pitchers, linens, whittling, lighting, domestic bric-a-brac, and national symbols — the latter two of which were among a few subsets that spun off into exhibitions at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. [65] Their exhibition catalogs are here: I Remember That: An Exhibition of Interiors of a Generation Ago (1942) and Emblems of Unity and Freedom (1945). The Emblems catalog notes that, “what is important” about these symbols “is not their immemorial origins, but the use which the American people have made of them” — a resonant message for our violently divisive present.

The project coordinators developed strict guidelines and drafted [66] a manual directing artists to strive for “accurate” and “faithful” representations, to adopt “exact” proportions, and to use specific kinds of paints and paper.[xii] Abby Foster of the National Gallery of Art, which now houses the collection, notes that the Index also includes several “instruction plates” that “show the process of [67] building up pigment on the paper to realistically achieve the texture of metal, wood, or fabric.”[xiii] This simulacral aspiration — wanting the images to feel like their subjects — thus transforms this index into another kind: the semiotic index. I hope you’ll pardon a little theoretical detour.

[68] Pragmatist philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce distinguished between different kinds of signs: Symbols, like those of the alphanumeric variety, don’t resemble the things to which they refer. The Arabic numeral six doesn’t look like a sextet of anything. Such symbols’ connection is conventional; it’s learned. Icons, like portraits and diagrams, resemble the things to which they refer. Indexes, then, are caused by, and serve as evidence or traces of, or they designate the existence of, the things they represent.[xiv] Weathervanes and thermometers and sundials — all represented in the Index of American Design — are indexes, as are paw prints, [69] an X-ray of a cancerous tumor, a rap on a door, smoke, the lingering scents of Upper East Side grand dames who’ve since left the room. Pointed fingers, too. Index fingers can themselves be indexes in the Peircian sense! [70] Yet as Guggenheim digital curator Noam Segal explains — I had the pleasure of serving on a panel with her at the Swiss Institute two months ago — artificial intelligence severs signs both temporally and causally from their referents, obsolescing the index and upending our standard semiotic models.[xv]

[71] In the days before the arrival of post-indexical agents, though, many of the Index of American Design’s paintings approximated, in texture, their referents — which foreshadows some of the material indexes we’ll encounter on Table #2. But for now I want to call your attention to the valiant work of the National Gallery of Art, which has [72] digitized and indexed all 18,000 works. Abby Foster and Matt Westerby, digital humanities scholars at the National Gallery, also generously shared [73] a bibliography — a cousin to the index — of over 100 published resources about the Index, and they’ve supported the creation of [74] a public interface to the image collection that pulls on collections metadata and AI-generated tags. Westerby, who kindly reached out to me to share their work, also informed me that he was planning to teach a spring class at the Corcoran called “Reimagining America by Design: The Speculative Index,” which would invite students to [75] “create digital exhibitions to accompany a small display of items from the the Archives of American Art and the vertical files of the National Gallery Library about the Index.” Sadly, I don’t see the class in the Corcoran’s spring catalog. A key question he wanted the students to ask, he told me, is: “what would be different if the Index collection and archives had been given to the Library of Congress instead of the National Gallery?”

The institutional context shapes what an index is and does. In 1940, after the Index of American Art had been terminated, Archibald MacLeish, the Librarian of Congress, approached Holger Cahill, director of the Federal Art Project, to ask if the Index materials could be deposited at the Library – but Cahill preferred that they be given to an institution where they’d be “exhibited frequently and cared for as works of art” — rather than as mere “documentation” of material culture. Cahill wanted them to be valued, and indexed, more for their material specificity and aesthetic value than for their “content.” Sounds a lot like contemporary critiques of LLMs. All of these considerations also echo Westerby’s concerns about what an index indexes, and whether that work is context-specific. Cahill originally bequeathed the renderings to the Met here in New York, but MacLeish thought they belonged in D.C.: this index was also a national treasure; it represented federal public knowledge. Ultimately, the Index landed at the National Gallery.[xvi] [76] As we see with DOGE’s obliviousness to context, and with the geographies of AI data centers, where the index originates and resides matters.

[77] Now, let’s step around the table to consider some other indices that, like the Index of American Design, are committed to indexing visual techniques and grammars, as much as they are the subjects in which those techniques are applied. [78] We have here J. G. Heck’s Iconographic Encyclopedia of Science, Literature, and Art (1851). Again, we see an inter-indexing of bibliographic labels: this encyclopedia is perhaps called that because of its exhaustive ambition, but it’s also an index. And it, like the Index we just saw, has also been digitized and, [79] thanks to data artist Nicholas Rougeaux, who has examined several historically significant diagrammatic texts, [80] it’s been indexed and analyzed.[xvii] This index has an index: [81] Rougeaux indexed the Encyclopedia’s figures into 18 subject areas.

[82] We should acknowledge a proliferation of contemporary visual indexes, like the DragonflyEye image bank by Now-Time, a semi-cult design studio perhaps best known for its [83] critical theory sweatshirts – [84] or the Cybernetics Image Library. Could it be that the explosion of non-indexical imagery is driving some folks to image indexes for assistance with sorting through the slop?

[85] We then have the Anaglypta Index of Architectural Ornament (1926). Anaglypta was a paper pulp material used in embossed wallpaper and as a substitute for plaster work. [86] Next, a canonical text featured in the museum’s 2023-24 “Give Me a Sign” exhibition: [87] Henry Dreyfuss’s Symbol Sourcebook: An Authoritative Guide to International Graphic Symbols (1972), is an attempt to classify an extensive, but not exhaustive, collection of symbols drawn from his Data Bank of 20,000 symbols; if Google were running the project, they might call it a Symbol Index. What we find inside is a mix of Peircian symbols and icons. [88] We move on now to Johann Ferdinand Ritter von Schönfeld’s Weiner Farbenkabinet (Manual on Preparation of Color) (1794), one of only four known copies in U.S. It contains 2,592 hand-colored natural dye specimens – which Peirce might regard as indices of their natural sources — along with details on how to apply them to various materials.

[89] We now move from color manual to color atlas: Paul Baumann’s Farbtonkarte Atlas II (1940) featuring index cards with color gradients. I unfortunately couldn’t find much scholarship on this work, but our progression from encyclopedia to index to sourcebook to manual to atlas makes me wonder about the organizational and epistemological claims being made by each bibliographic form! Now, another index: [90] Susan Winter Mills’s Illustrated Index to Traditional American Quilt Patterns (1980), which she describes as a “reference tool for [her] own quiltmaking – something to thumb through, like a catalog, a method more conducive to inspiration.” In producing her index / reference tool / catalog, she cross-indexed graphic patterns and their place-specific names: “collecting as many names as possible,” she writes, “is the only sensible way to index patterns that may be known by different names.”

[91] Moving on: Jim Krause’s collection of design indexes, beginning with his Idea Index: Graphic Effects and Typographic Treatments (2000): “By placing hundreds of visual and conceptual suggestions directly before the artist’s eyes and mind,” he writes, “Idea Index stimulates, quickens and expands the creative process…. This book is a tool that stocks the creative reservoir, brings useful ideas to the surface and offers the spark needed to make a good idea great.” An index is a tool, a stockpile, a reservoir, an ignition spark. He followed the Idea index up with a Layout Index (2001), a Design Basic Index (2004), and a Color Index (2002).

[92] Now, moving on to Table 2, we shift from the visual to the material; surpassing the Index of American Design’s aspiration to simulate texture, these resources incorporate texture — texture you can see and feel with your own index finger. Extending our collection of color indexes, [93] we look now at the Standard Color Reference of America (1981), a book of textile samples first issued in 1915 to aid in the standardization of colorwork. The American flag and many state flags — among the patriotic symbols represented in the Index of American Design Emblems of Unity and Freedom exhibition — are among the textile works based on the Standard Color Reference. We now turn to one of my favorites: [94] American Fabrics magazine, which chronicled 40 years of the textile and fashion industries in the U.S., from 1946 through 1983. These vibrantly designed oversized periodicals featured copious [95] “tipped in,” or glued in, indexical samples, [96] as well as analog interactive features — some of which we’ll see at Table #3 — and a range of paper stocks, to enhance the haptic experience. [97] Trimming away all the editorial frills is this Knoll Textiles sample card and its cousin: [98] the WallClad wallpaper book, where we can see, feel, and smell the wares before slapping them up on our walls.

American Fabrics treated not only fabric, but also the paper it was printed on, as a multisensory medium. The same was true of a periodical of a different scale: [99] the diminutive PM Magazine, a nonprofit periodical published between 1934 and 1942 to serve print production managers and art directors. [100] It not only described but also modeled — in indexical fashion — [101] printing processes, typefaces, and materials.[xviii] It featured the work of many American and emigre designers, too. [102] Cardboard (Nat-Mat Cardboards) and [CLICK] endpapers also have their own indexes. [103] Rosamind Loring’s Decorated Book Papers: Being an Account of Their Designs and Fashions (1942) includes many tipped-in samples, accompanied by texts on the history and technicalities of decorative papers — it’s thus an index of various material fabrication processes — as well as a list of early paper makers. Finally, another favorite, even more diminutive than American Fabrics — an often overlooked, tiny, quotidian medium: [104] the matchbook. The Match Corporation of America’s sample book demonstrates their product as a portable advertisement, a status marker, a calling card, a travel souvenir, a carrier of the traces of its own use: what a versatile indexical medium.

[105] The index finger and the thumb activate the matchbook, which might ignite a candle or a lantern to illuminate a book — or might light a bonfire to incinerate an archive or consume a hoard of banned books. The match engages the fingers in knowledge work. Our next section featured additional materials that demonstrate indexing as tactile work, work engaging nimble fingers and sensitive fingertips. [106] Let’s start with Vladimir Mayakovsky + El Lissitzky’s For the Voice (1923). As the Smithsonian’s own Liz O’Brien explained, this 61-page booklet

[107] rhythmically interlaces innovative constructivist style layouts and patterns with thirteen futurist poems… Mayakovsky, like Lissitzky, emphasized the shape of letters, the placement of text on a page, and the importance of typography over traditional grammar, syntax, and logic. He felt that designing the spatial arrangement of a poet’s words on the page is akin to that of an artist arranging colors and lines on a canvas.[xix]

Meanwhile, Lissitzky’s pages, he says, “stand in much the same relationship to the poems as an accompanying piano to a violin. Just as the poet unites concepts and sound, I have tried to create an equivalent unity using the poem and typography.” [108] The bibliographic form is an instrument, too: Lissitzky has designed a system of tabs with a distinctive symbol for each poem, as if each has its own note on a piano keyboard.

Index-fingering through tabs is also central to the work of filing — [109][110][111] as exemplified in these rolodexes and file indexes in the Cooper Hewitt’s collection. [112] My friend and colleague Craig Robetson, who’s written about the history of information labor, explains how, in the early 20th century, filing was framed as gendered manual — and not necessarily intellectual — labor. In his article, “Learning to File,” Craig describes how “a file clerk’s hands and fingers became central to the representation and teaching of filing. In this way, filing offered an example of a distinctly modern form of information work. Filing textbooks sought to enhance dexterity.” [113] He quotes someone from a vocational education firm: “It is generally agreed that women do well at painstaking, tedious work requiring patience and dexterity of the hands. The actual fact that women’s fingers are more slender than men’s makes a difference.” Another manager stated that they “often ask a girl if she plays the piano, or if she knits, crochets, sews, or does another type of work that would enable her to acquire speed with her fingers.”[xx] [114] Some of artist Kelli Anderdon’s indexical gadgets and riso animations exemplify these principles. [115] Kelli, as I said earlier, joined me for the public program.

Now, let’s look at the indexical, mechanical referent for Craig’s scholarship and Kelli’s artwork. [116] What we see here is the card catalog of George Adolf Kubler, founder and president of Certified Dry Mat Corporation, which made stereoplates for printing newspapers. They cast metal plates from papier-mâché or plaster moulds called flongs,which is a wonderful word. In the early 20th century, Kubler also collected and cataloged prints; he clipped, mounted, filed, and indexed over 60,000 images drawn from European and American magazines, newspapers, and books. Topics ranged from boxing, churches, dry docks, funerals, and irrigation to milk peddlers, volcanoes, and wrecks. He included portraits, city views, and surveys of occupations and historical events. This card catalog, and others like it in the closed stacks, is the only means to access the prints. As library director Jen Bracchi explains in a blog post appropriately titled “Before Google Images,” Kubler’s cataloging system is “almost exclusively by subject with no regard for artist, engraver, or source of the picture.”[xxi] As with current-day generative AI, we don’t know where all the harvested data comes from! We can’t point toward sources.

[117] We can then of course scale up this tiny card catalog up to the scale of the filing cabinet, the subject of Craig’s most recent book. As a sidenote, I’ll index my own writing about the play of filing and the aesthetic and logics of book storage. Speaking of furnishings: we can also look to [118] this Space Saver catalog and brochure, and this Stendig poster, which index their own equipment for indexing labor.

[119] We’ll drop a footnote — or, rather, a finger-note — here for a sub-category of manual knowledge: needlework. We can connect a thread back to the quilt index from Table 1. But here, we see indexes of patterns for tatting, crochet, knitting, netting, embroidery, lace, Berlin work, monograms, and more. [120]Those patterns are indexical in that they bear a causal relationship to the resulting textile works. And of course samplers and quilts and tapestries and quipu are knowledge objects; they tell stories and document things and stitch together histories and hold secrets. In the interest of time, we won’t look individually at these materials — you’ll have more time to explore at the end of our tour — [121] but I’ll highlight what we have here: Beeton’s Book of Needlework (1870); and The Workwoman’s Guide: Instructions to the Inexperienced in Cutting Out and Completing Those Articles of Weaving Apparel, Which Are Usually Made at Home (1838), which features a visual index at the back. We also have La Fleur des Patrons De Lingerie (The Flower of Lingerie Patterns) a Deux Endroitz, a Point Croise, a Point Colx’he, et a Pointe Picque, en Fil D’or (1873); History of Needlework Tools; [122] and another of those indexical sample catalogs, the Dosco Needle Catalog, which includes tools that engage the fingers in material knowledge work.

[123] These needles point us toward our third and final table, where we’ll explore more tactile modes of bibliographic engagement. [124] We start with Andrew Gardenier’s Geometrie Stereographique, Reliefs Des Polyedres (King Richardson Publishing, 1855), which presents an early-19th-century form of descriptive geometry adapted to manual instruction; the book features pre-cut geometric shapes engraved on cardboard that the reader can fold into Euclidean bodies. Next door is the Handbook of Ready Reference (1897), a veterinary guidebook with paper models of a horse and cow. [125] Preceding and besting both of these titles is Petrus Apianus’s Astronomicus Caesarium, the Emperor’s Astronomy (1540 / 1969); two Holy Roman emperors commissioned the work, which features volvelles that upstage the book’s text. According to Ronald Brashear and Daniel Lewis, Astronomicum is “really a scientific calculating instrument as much as a book.”[xxii]

Books can invite our fingers to do more than flip, fold, flap, and spin. [126] In his Surprise Book (1941), Tony Sarg, a German-American puppeteer and illustrator who also designed balloons and windows for Macy’s, incorporated volvelles, strokeable sheep, and pluckable instrument strings, engaging young readers through all the senses. [CLICK] One of Sarg’s predecessors in the interactive children’s book terrain was Lothar Meggendorffer, who created more than 200 pop-up and moveable books involving pull-tabs and levers. Neue Lebende Bilder (188X) invites us to manipulate the page to help a girl draw water from a well, a painter paint a portrait, a woman wash clothes, a musician play a cello, a butcher chop meat, and a dog learn a new trick.

Kelli Anderson’s books synthesize these traditions: paper engineering, interaction as play, book as instrument. We featured her [127] This Book is a Planetarium, which the Cooper Hewitt has in its collection, and her brand-new book, Alphabet In Motion [128]

[129] We’ll close this penultimate section with a final, elementary example: the manual for the Palmer Method of Business Writing, appreciated for its plainness, speed, and discipline — qualities that are precisely the opposite of those espoused by and embodied in the previous examples. Nevertheless, this manual engages the hand in, if not the creation of new knowledge, then in the production of new bureaucratic paperwork — precisely the kind of writing that LLMs seem to be good for.

Now, as we close out our tour, we home in on the micro scale: the index finger itself. It’s well represented in the Cooper Hewitt’s collection: [130] The finger gesticulating, maybe asking sheepishly  to be called on in class, perhaps prompting a companion to “wait a minute.” [131] The imperiled finger offering a rebuke to those who spilt secrets or snitched — which, by the way, LLMs are very good at, too. [132] The finger pushing a button — itself a major development in the history of interaction. [133] The finger holding place in a book. [134] The finger marking a passage in a text. [135] The finger pointing out has long been a motif in study: we see here some manicules drawn in the margins of manuscripts to mark passages of note. [136] And here: a Jewish Yad, a pointer tipped with an extended finger, which allows a reader to guide their passage though the sacred Torah without touching the text. [137] Everyone at my September event at the Cooper Hewitt got a manicule on a stick and a souvenir set of creepy golden hands book clamps.

While these all represent the hand of the reader, [138] we find in the Nuremberg Chronicle (1492 Latin / 1493 German) — printed into the text itself rather than added as unofficial marginalia — the hand of god, [CLICK] clearly a model for today’s tech elite. [CLICK] Written by physician / humanist Hartmann Schedel (1440-1514), the Chronicle offers a universal history of the Christian world; it’s among the most extensively illustrated German incunables, or cradle texts. The authoritative manicule becomes a motif. [139] We regularly find it in type specimen books, like this one from 1897. [140] It’s been adopted as a skeuomorphic representation of our engagement with the screen. [141] We even find fingers in our digital books: here the be-finger-gloved ghost hands of book scanners who accidentally remind us of the manual infrastructures supporting our purportedly automated, immaterial world.

[141] But the hand itself has also been a keeper of memory, an interface to the soul, a spiritual text.[xxiii] [143] The fingers, too, are indexes of agency and signaling tools, [144] as we can see here in Kelli’s manual protest models. [145] The index finger can also register refusal — including, perhaps, [146] the rejection of technologies nobody asked for.

[147] The index of the index finger — the fingerprint — has been weaponized by criminologists and eugenicists.[xxiv] This kind of physiognomic profiling is newly and frighteningly resurgent in this age of sanctioned and algorithmically amplified quackery and cruelty. [148] But the print is also an indexical trace of presence, of contact, of pressure, [149] as we see in Sam Gassman’s Finger Print Book, whose “content” is nothing but traces of touch. They remind us that individual hands can play a hand in rewriting the books, redrawing the map — by showing up to library board meetings or creating hand-drawn protest placards or throwing sandwiches… or refusing to click. [150] These prints prompt us to ask how we can recognize, and fight for, the human hands that pick our vegetables and clean our hotel rooms and write the books that so often then feed the rapacious plagiarism machines.

To index is to interpellate, to call out, to call back, to hold accountable, to give credit, to leave a mark, a trace. In Caoilinn Hughes’s short story, “A Woman of No Information,” a filmmaker implores his colleagues to ditch their scripts: “A different story needs a new way of telling it… You know the exact moment a sculptor makes a masterpiece? When the clay is wet in his hands. Fuck the mould. I want a story with fingerprints on it.”[xxv] In a world of glaring screens and sycophantic bots, we need more fingerprinted indexes ([151] not more cloudified indexes of fingerprints and other personally identifiable information – including [152] Grammerly’s recent experts index, which is a perverted form of citation). [153] We can find inspiration in those who deobfuscate the index’s form, calling attention to the index’s existence and logics, its politics and poetics.[xxvi] [154] Plus, we’re seeing more indexes of strategies for resistance and principled refusal.

Even the cloud itself offers opportunities for reparative indexing. [155] I think of an installation I saw on the Lower East Side back in 2013. Cynthia Daignault’s “I Love You More Than One Day” featured 365 10” x 15” paintings of the sky over the course of one year. As you can see here, I likened the composite work to an “Empyrian Index.” [156] I used to write blog posts about all of my gallery excursions, but over the years, as my service and advising loads began to crush me, I ran out of time to sustain this reflective practice — which makes me appreciate all the more Daignault’s example of discipline and practice and careful observation. [157] These aren’t photos: they’re paintings with brushstrokes and fingerprints.

[158] Cloudspotting for Beginners, published by the Cloud Appreciation Society’s Gavin Pretor-Pinney and illustrator William Grill in 2024, [159] indexes the formal, chromatic, climatic, geographic, and other variables we should be attuned to when “spotting” clouds — [160] which, again, are illustrated through fingerprinted illustrations. [161] I also think of Christine Tyler Hill’s The Cloud Report zine, in which she documents observations from her vantage as a crossing guard in Burlington, VT. Again, lots of personal and local fingerprints. [162] As an aside, Elisabeth Nicula, in her new publication, the San Francisco Review of Whatever, has set aside the centerfold to a “Cloud Interlude,” and invites curators to interpret that term as they wish.

[163] Earlier this week I attended a wonderful two-day symposium on indigenous librarianship at Bard. There, Marisa Duarte described indigenous knowledges as “a guide left to indigenous people by their elders indexing how to sustain our ways of knowing.” Indexing. I interpreted this deliberate word choice to mean that these knowledges are rooted in place, germinated by their contexts, born of the soil and clouds. They’re traces of the communities and terrains that cultivate and steward them. [164] The indigenous principle of land-based knowing resonates with data scientist Yanni Loukissas’s assertion that all data are local: they have settings, they’re rooted in place and community – and using them responsibly requires recognition of this fact.

[165] Attunement to place also prepares us to acknowledge the soils and clouds themselves as embodiments of intelligence — the kind that need to be experienced in their full, situated materiality, observed and appraised through sensitivities cultivated across generations. Traces of knowing drawn across time. [166] Clouds, like indexes and other epistemological forms, have the potential to be capacious, convivial, relational, creative entities. Recognizing this multifariousness helps us appreciate our power to imagine things otherwise, to build more reparative, responsive systems.

[167] Which brings us to our final example, regarding clouds’ own indexical traces — that is, the raindrops evidencing their presence above. Last year MIT Press published Miya Ando’s Water of the Sky: A Dictionary of 2000 Japanese Rain Words, each illustrated with natural indigo, micronized silver, and graphite — a material assemblage indexing the elemental materiality of its referent. There’s no single ontology uniting the book’s contents, [168] which range “from the meteorological (mukaame, ‘very fine rain that falls in spring’) to the mystical (bunryūu, ‘rain that splits a dragon’s body in half’), and from the delicate (kisame, ‘raindrops that fall off leaves and branches’) to the vast (takuu, ‘blessed rain that quenches all things in the universe’).” As Ando explains, “the work transforms a dictionary into a perceptual system: an index capturing rain’s multifaceted physical, emotional, and temporal dimensions.” She pairs the index-as-bibliographic-form – which typically requires standardization — with the index-as-evidentiary-mark-making to demonstrate slippages in translation and place-based knowing. Rain, Ando shows, saturates a culture and its symbolic forms, creating a system of relationality and cyclical accountability that would drown any artificial agent. As those bots disrupt the water cycle and precipitate environmental destruction and global terror that will materially impact the clouds above, I hope we can find the profound wisdom in an index of raindrops. I hope we’ll fight to preserve the place-based knowledge, poetic sensitivities, and ecological intelligence — and accountability — it exemplifies. [169]
